Subject: Questions on token counting semantics for hosted API

Hi Sean,

We're getting internal procurement and engineering aligned for a pilot with Redwood. Before we start legal and sizing, we need to confirm a few billing semantics so our cost modeling is accurate. Can you confirm the following?

1) System vs user tokens: if we send a standard system message (role: system) plus user messages, are the system prompt tokens included in the input token tally for billing?

2) Tool/function calls: if the model returns a function call (JSON payload) and we later pass that payload back into another request (or store it in our DB), how are those tokens accounted for? Does the returned JSON count as output tokens when generated and then as input tokens if reused?

3) Rounding: when you bill tokens, do you round per request, per second, or per-minute buckets? Example: three tiny requests that each produce 2.3 tokens — are they rounded individually or aggregated before rounding?

4) Streaming & partial tokens: for streamed responses, are partial tokens billed as soon as emitted, or is final tokenization used?

5) Batching behavior: if we send batched payloads (multiple user contexts concatenated into a single API call for throughput), how does that affect per-user cost accounting?

I've attached a short example log excerpt to illustrate (example_log_snippet.txt). Also, for quoting, please include a sample per-1M input/output token baseline so I can show numbers to procurement.

Thanks — happy to jump on a quick call if that helps.

Jane — thanks for the clear list. Below are concise answers and a few examples; I'll follow up with a short FAQ PDF and a draft ratecard workbook attached.

Quick answers (short):
- System tokens: yes — any text you send as part of the request (system, user, assistant messages included in the request payload) is counted as input tokens.
- Returned tool/function payloads: generation of the function call (name + JSON payload that the model emits) is billed as output tokens. If you later include that JSON as part of a new request, those tokens are counted again as input for that new request.
- Rounding: we round at the request level — we sum the exact token counts (input + output) for each API call and meter/round that total for billing. We do not aggregate across separate API calls for rounding purposes.
- Streaming: billing is based on the tokens actually generated by the model. Partial/emitted tokens are counted once they are produced; final tokenization does not change what has already been emitted and billed.
- Batching: if you intentionally concatenate multiple user contexts into a single API call (i.e., you build a single request with multiple conversation blocks), we bill the total tokens in that combined request. To preserve per-user economics, send separate API calls per logical user and rely on Redwood's runtime batching to optimize throughput — our runtime batches requests for GPU efficiency but preserves per-request accounting.

Examples (approx.):
- Request A: system(40 tokens) + user(120 tokens) => model generates 300 tokens. Billing: input=160, output=300, billed on the request total (460 tokens).
- Function call: model emits function name + JSON (e.g., "search_results": 220 tokens) => those 220 tokens are output. If you store that JSON and later include it in a subsequent request, that reuse will add those tokens to input for the new request.
- Rounding example: three separate calls with totals 2.3, 1.7, 3.4 tokens are each rounded at request level (so 3, 2, 4 tokens respectively). We do not sum them to 7.4 then round to 7.

Caveats and best practices:
- Tokenization differs per model; exact byte-to-token mapping can vary for edge cases (special characters, long code blocks). We provide a tokenization tool in the Console to validate counts per model.
- If you have tool invocations whose output you re-ingest frequently, consider storing a compressed canonical representation (or caching server-side) and referencing via ID to avoid repeated re-ingestion billing.

Attached: token-counting-faq.pdf and a proposed-ratecard-draft.xlsx with baseline numbers. Happy to hop on a 30m call tomorrow to walk through the examples.

Jane — quick clarifications below; I've also looped in Marissa (pricing) and Ben (sales ops) on a follow-up for a formal pilot quote.

A) Redwood-hosted tools/proxies: we bill for tokens generated by the model the same way irrespective of whether a tool is involved. If a tool's content is included in the model's output payload returned to you, that counts as model output tokens. There is not a separate token bucket for "tool I/O" — it's all model input/output. If we invoke external services on your behalf and they return content that the model then emits, that result is billed as output tokens.

B) Signalling per-user boundaries: there is not a protocol-level flag in a single request to make the runtime treat different segments as separate billing entities. Billing is per API call. Two recommended approaches:
  - Send logical per-user requests and allow Redwood's runtime to batch at the GPU layer (this preserves per-request billing and is simplest).
  - If you must submit a concatenated request for throughput, accept that billing will be for the total tokens in that request; you can still record per-user offsets client-side for your internal chargebacks, but Redwood will produce one invoice line for that API call.

C) Example baseline pricing (illustrative; final quote from Sales Ops):
  - Baseline list price (hosted API): $2.00 per 1M input tokens, $4.00 per 1M output tokens.
  - Example: 1M input + 1M output => $6.00 before discounts.

Notes on discounts: committed monthly usage can materially reduce effective unit prices. For pilots we commonly offer a time-limited consumption credit and commit to a 10–20% pilot discount on list for an initial term; larger committed ARR replaces the pilot discount with an enterprise tier pricing schedule.
